mechanism_chain.process: Occupant enters a building whose spatial layout matches a stored architectural schema (e.g., 'hospital layout', 'school corridor plan', 'office grid'). Neocortical schema is activated via prefrontal-hippocampal interaction.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) schema representation → hippocampal encoding modulation
mechanism_chain.source: Tse et al. (2007); van Kesteren et al. (2012)

data.finding: mPFC activation during encoding increases when new information is schema-consistent; mPFC-hippocampal connectivity predicts schema-facilitated learning
data.effect: mPFC mediates schema effects on encoding

data.finding: Rats with pre-existing spatial schema (event arena) show rapid single-trial learning of new locations within the schema

justification.backing: Morris and colleagues established that neocortical schemas (stored in mPFC) can accelerate new learning by providing a pre-existing framework. The mPFC-hippocampal interaction determines whether new information is encoded via slow hippocampal-dependent or fast schema-dependent pathways.
justification.qualifier: The schema mechanism is established; the application to architectural schemas (hospital layout, office grid) involves inference from general schema research to building-specific knowledge structures.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if architectural schemas are too weak or variable to support schema-dependent encoding; first-time building users may lack relevant schemas.

mechanism_chain.process: Activated schema provides a pre-existing framework: new spatial information (specific room locations, service positions) is rapidly assimilated into the schema structure, bypassing the slow hippocampal-dependent encoding process
mechanism_chain.substrate: Neocortical schema → accelerated hippocampal binding; reduced hippocampal dependency for schema-consistent information
mechanism_chain.source: Tse et al. (2007); Tse et al. (2011)

data.finding: Hippocampal lesions impair new learning ONLY when no schema exists; with pre-existing schema, neocortex can support rapid new learning independently of hippocampus
Schema-consistent information reaches stable neocortical representation within hours rather than weeks

justification.backing: Tse et al. demonstrated that schemas fundamentally change the dynamics of memory encoding: when a schema exists, new information can be rapidly integrated without the slow hippocampal-dependent consolidation process that typically takes weeks.
justification.qualifier: The acceleration effect is demonstrated in rodents with artificially constructed schemas. Human architectural schemas are acquired more naturalistically; the degree of acceleration may vary.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if human architectural schemas are less coherent than experimental animal schemas; real building types may have more variability than laboratory event arenas.

mechanism_chain.process: Schema-consistent information is encoded ~50% faster but with lower distinctiveness (weaker hippocampal trace, stronger neocortical trace). Schema-inconsistent information generates prediction errors and is encoded more slowly but with higher distinctiveness (stronger hippocampal trace).
mechanism_chain.source: Tse et al. (2007); Greve et al. (2017)

data.finding: Schema-consistent items are learned faster but remembered less distinctively; schema-inconsistent items are learned slower but remembered more distinctively
data.paradigm: Human schema learning with memory tests

data.finding: Schema violation produces prediction error signal that enhances hippocampal encoding (similar to novelty effect)
data.source: van Kesteren et al. (2012); prediction error literature

justification.backing: The schema presents a tradeoff: conformity enables fast learning but produces less distinctive memories (prone to interference). Violation triggers prediction error that enhances encoding distinctiveness at the cost of learning speed.
justification.qualifier: The 50% faster estimate is derived from laboratory schema paradigms. The distinctiveness-speed tradeoff in architectural contexts is inferred rather than directly measured.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if architectural users prioritize speed over distinctiveness regardless of design; wayfinding in unfamiliar buildings may demand schema conformity even at the cost of memorability.

schema_conformity_priority.interpretation: fast_encoding: maximize schema conformity → ~50% faster spatial learning, lower distinctiveness. deep_encoding: moderate schema violation → ~30% slower learning, higher distinctiveness and memorability.

hippocampal_encoding.interpretation: Features that violate the activated schema are encoded ~25% more strongly (but ~30% more slowly) than schema-consistent features

schema_availability_threshold.interpretation: Schema activation requires prior experience with the building type; first-time visitors to a hospital do not have a 'hospital schema' and cannot benefit from schema-dependent acceleration

expertise_familiarity.effect: Architects, wayfinding designers, and frequent travelers have richer and more diverse spatial schemas; schema acceleration is stronger for these populations

cognitive_impairment.effect: Schema retrieval is impaired in early-stage dementia; schema-dependent acceleration is reduced or absent. Schema-conforming design is STILL beneficial (simpler layout) but the acceleration mechanism operates at reduced capacity.

IC2_AX4_interaction.IC2_body_budget: Allostatic load impairs prefrontal cortex function, which is required for schema retrieval and activation. Under body budget deficit, schema-dependent acceleration is reduced because the mPFC cannot efficiently activate the stored schema. This creates a double jeopardy in stressful environments: occupants who most need fast spatial learning (e.g., emergency patients) are least able to benefit from schema acceleration.
IC2_AX4_interaction.AX4_perceived_control: High perceived control facilitates schema activation by reducing prefrontal cognitive load. Environments that signal predictability and control (clear signage, visible exits, orderly layout) support both AX4 and schema-dependent encoding simultaneously.

ED_SYSTEMS_CONSOLIDATION_001 — schema availability accelerates systems consolidation (Tse et al., 2007)
ED_HIPPOCAMPAL_ENCODING_001 — schema conformity trades off against encoding distinctiveness

spatial_configuration.interpretation: Degree to which spatial layout matches the prototypical layout for the building type; higher typicality → stronger schema activation → faster encoding

age_group.interpretation: Signage and wayfinding cues that match schematic expectations (e.g., green exit signs, numbered floor indicators) reinforce schema activation

name: Schema-Dependent Encoding in Architectural Environments
